newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon court jails Japanese Red Army guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon court jails Japanese Red Army guerrillas.

text.p: A Lebanese court on Thursday sentenced five Japanese Red Army guerrillas to three years each in jail on charges relating to their illegal stay in the country.
The four men and one woman, who had been arrested in Beirut in February, were not brought to the court to hear the verdicts and sentences announced.
The five were convicted on different charges, including forging official stamps, illegal entry into Lebanon and forging passports, but all received three-year sentences.
The decision came one day after the United States lifted a 10-year-old ban on its citizens visiting Lebanon after receiving pledges from Beirut that it would do more to fight "terrorism".
All five had been on an international wanted list because of their guerrilla activities dating back to the 1970s.

The prisoners included Kozo Okamoto, who joined two comrades in a 1972 machinegun and grenade attack inside Tel Aviv's Lod airport in which 26 people died, including his two companions. He was captured but released by Israel in a 1985 prisoner exchange.
Okamoto and Haruo Wako received only jail sentences. Masao Adachi, Mariko Yamamoto and Kazuo Tohira were also fined 600,000 Lebanese pounds ($390).
Defence lawyers said they would appeal the sentences at a higher court.
"The court ruled unanimously that forging official documents and using them was an offence...and convicted Adachi, Yamamoto and Tohira of this offence," said judge Suheil Abdel Samad.
Okamoto and Wako were acquitted of these charges but all five were convicted of entering the country with forged passports and forged visas.

The judge said the prisoners would be deported after their sentences but did not specify where they might go. Japan initially had sought their extradition. Japan and Lebanon do not have an extradition agreement.
The court rejected the guerrillas' defence that their crimes in Lebanon had been political. The defendants had asked for their release and the granting of political asylum.

"The motive was a personal and selfish interest that would allow them to stay in Lebanon regardless of their beliefs, though the court appreciates the heroic act one of the defendants (Okamoto) executed against the Israeli enemy," the judge said.
"They could have asked for political asylum instead of using forged passports to enter the country."

The court acquitted Lebanese acupuncturist Umayya Abboud of charges of illegally practising medicine. Abboud, arrested with the guerrillas last February, was originally accused of helping them forge documents but the charges were dropped later.

The Red Army, founded in 1971, was allied to hardline anti-Israeli Palestinian factions. Many of its guerrillas stayed in the Bekaa Valley which during Lebanon's 1975-1990 civil war was a haven for guerrilla groups including Lebanese Moslems and Marxists, Palestinians, Kurds and the Red Army.
